facts.statement: Chindesaurus lived in the southwestern United States during the Late Triassic, approximately 213 to 210 million years ago.
facts.quote: Chindesaurus ( ) is an extinct genus of basal saurischian dinosaur from the Late Triassic (213-210 million years ago) of the southwestern United States.

facts.statement: Chindesaurus was a bipedal carnivore roughly the size of a wolf.
facts.quote: Chindesaurus was a bipedal carnivore, approximately as large as a wolf.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Chindesaurus was discovered in 1984 by Bryan Small in a blue mudstone layer within Petrified Forest National Park.
facts.quote: PEFO 10395 was discovered in 1984 by Bryan Small, who recovered the skeleton from a blue mudstone layer in the Chinle Formation's Upper Petrified Forest Member.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, nicknamed "Gertie," was airlifted by helicopter on June 6, 1985, to the University of California Museum of Paleontology for preparation.
facts.quote: "Gertie" was subsequently airlifted by helicopter on June 6, 1985, and brought to the University of California Museum of Paleontology (UCMP) in Berkeley, CA, where it was prepared over the next several years.

facts.statement: Chindesaurus was formally described and named by R.A. Long and P.A. Murry in 1995.
facts.quote: "Gertie" was described and given a binomial name by R.A. Long and P.A. Murry in 1995.

facts.statement: The genus name Chindesaurus combines the location "Chinde Point" with the Greek word for lizard.
facts.quote: The generic name combines Chinde Point with the Greek word "sauros" (σαυρος) (meaning "lizard").

facts.statement: The species name bryansmalli honors the discoverer of the skeleton, Bryan Small.
facts.quote: The specific name, bryansmalli, honors Bryan Small, who discovered the skeleton.

facts.statement: Long and Murry estimated Chindesaurus had a stout body, long legs, and a length of 3 to 4 meters.
facts.quote: Long & Murry reconstructed Chindesaurus with a stout body, long legs, a fairly long neck, and a total estimated length of 3 to 4 m.

facts.statement: Holtz (2012) estimated Chindesaurus was about 2 meters long and weighed between 23 and 45 kilograms.
facts.quote: Holtz (2012) estimated that Chindesaurus had a length of about 2 meters (6.6) feet and a weight equivalent to that of a wolf (23–45 kg, or about 50-100 pounds).

facts.statement: The holotype specimen may not have been fully grown, as indicated by unfused ankle and dorsal neurocentral sutures.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen may not be fully grown due to its unfused ankle and dorsal neurocentral sutures.

facts.statement: A 2019 study suggested Chindesaurus was a theropod closely related to Tawa.
facts.quote: A 2019 redescription of its holotype considered Chindesaurus to be a theropod closely related to Tawa, a slightly smaller dinosaur known from the Hayden Quarry of Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.

facts.statement: A 2026 study placed Chindesaurus in a new clade called Morphoraptora, grouping it with Tawa as non-herrerasaurid herrerasaurians.
facts.quote: A 2026 study named the new clade Morphoraptora, consolidating Chindesaurus, Tawa, and other enigmatic southwestern saurischians into a single lineage of non-herrerasaurid herrerasaurians.

facts.statement: Native American staff and consultants have long opposed the name "Chinde Point" due to its association with a taboo concept in the Navajo language.
facts.quote: Native American staff and consultants of the national park have long voiced disapproval over the name of Chinde Point.

facts.statement: The name "Chinde Point" was replaced by "Hózhó Point" in September 2023 following approval by several Native American tribes.
facts.quote: A new name, Hózhó Point, was proposed in 2019 and formally adopted in September 2023, after approval by the Navajo, Hopi, Zuni, Tohono O'odham, and Pascua Yaqui.

facts.statement: The trunk vertebrae of Chindesaurus were deep, wide, and short, resembling herrerasaurids more than Tawa or coelophysoids.
facts.quote: The dorsal (trunk) vertebrae are deep, wide, and fairly short (from front-to-back), closer to the condition in herrerasaurids rather than Tawa and coelophysoids.

facts.statement: Neural spines in Chindesaurus expanded outward and backward to form "spine-tables," a structure also found in Herrerasaurus and Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: Neural spines expand outwards and backwards, forming "spine-tables", structures which are otherwise only observed in Herrerasaurus and Dilophosaurus among potential theropods.

facts.statement: The two preserved sacral vertebrae of Chindesaurus were wide and not fused to each other.
facts.quote: The two preserved sacral (hip) vertebrae are wide and not fused to each other.

facts.statement: The presence of only two unfused sacral vertebrae has been a key feature supporting the classification of Chindesaurus as a herrerasaurid.
facts.quote: The assumption that Chindesaurus had only two sacrals has been vital to its traditional identity as a herrerasaurid.

facts.statement: Large sacral ribs extended outward from the front half of each sacral vertebra in Chindesaurus.
facts.quote: Large sacral ribs extend outwards from the front half of each sacral vertebrae.

facts.statement: The tail vertebrae of Chindesaurus were large at the base and elongated toward the tip.
facts.quote: The caudal (tail) vertebrae are large at the base of the tail and elongated towards the tip of the tail.

facts.statement: The pubis bone of Chindesaurus was thin, straight, slightly curved backward, and widened toward the ilium.
facts.quote: The pubis is thin, straight, and slightly curved back, widening slightly towards the ilium.

facts.statement: The femur of Chindesaurus was large, sigmoid in shape, and possessed a smooth, rectangular femoral head.
facts.quote: The femur is large and sigmoid, with a smooth, rectangular femoral head.

facts.statement: The anterior trochanter of the Chindesaurus femur appeared as a bulbous ridge continuous with the shaft, lacking a separating cleft.
facts.quote: The anterior trochanter has the appearance of a bulbous ridge, not separated from the shaft by a cleft.

facts.statement: The lower end of the Chindesaurus femur had two distinct condyles that were triangular in cross-section.
facts.quote: The lower end of the femur has two distinct condyles which are triangular in cross-section.

facts.statement: The cnemial crest on the front of the Chindesaurus tibia was very low, measuring less than 35% of the bone's total anteroposterior thickness.
facts.quote: The cnemial crest running down the front of the tibia is quite low, <35% the total anteroposterior thickness of the bone.

facts.statement: The front edge of the Chindesaurus astragalus had a deep and broad cleft that subdivided the bone vertically.
facts.quote: The front edge of the astragalus has a deep and broad cleft which subdivides the bone vertically.

facts.statement: When first discovered in 1984, the fossil specimen of Chindesaurus was initially thought to be a prosauropod.
facts.quote: When it was first discovered in 1984, the fossil specimen which would eventually be named Chindesaurus was thought to be a "prosauropod" (basal sauropodomorph).

facts.statement: Chindesaurus was formally described and named in 1995 by Long and Murry, who classified it as a herrerasaurid.
facts.quote: When it was finally described and named a decade later by Long & Murry (1995), they regarded it as a herrerasaurid.

facts.statement: A partial ilium originally assigned to Chindesaurus was later classified as a separate species, Caseosaurus crosbyensis, by Hunt et al. (1998).
facts.quote: A partial ilium originally assigned to Chindesaurus, from the Tecovas Formation of Texas, was later placed in its own genus and species, Caseosaurus crosbyensis, by Hunt et al. (1998).

facts.statement: Research suggested that the Chindesaurus and Tawa clade belonged to basal Saurischia, before the split between sauropodomorphs and theropods.
facts.quote: Instead, it placed the Chindesaurus + Tawa clade within basal Saurischia, prior to the split between sauropodomorphs and theropods.

facts.statement: The sister-taxon relationship between Chindesaurus and Tawa was supported by a unique trait: a posterior margin on the proximal tibia divided by two notches.
facts.quote: Their sister-taxon relationship was supported by one apomorphy, or unique derived trait: a posterior margin of the proximal end of the tibia which is divided by two notches.

facts.statement: Srivastava and Nesbitt (2026) grouped Chindesaurus, Tawa, Daemonosaurus, and Ptychotherates into a new clade named Morphoraptora.
facts.quote: Srivastava & Nesbitt (2026) grouped Chindesaurus, Tawa, Daemonosaurus, and the new genus Ptychotherates into a newly named clade, Morphoraptora.

facts.statement: Langer (2004) argued that Caseosaurus and Chindesaurus likely represent the same species rather than distinct genera.
facts.quote: Langer (2004) argued that this separation was probably in error, and that the two forms represent the same species.

facts.statement: Nesbitt et al. (2007) supported the idea that differences between Caseosaurus and Chindesaurus were likely due to size-related variation.
facts.quote: Nesbitt et al. (2007) corroborated this, stating that the differences between Caseosaurus and Chindesaurus cited by Hunt et al. (1998) were probably a result of size-related variation.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Chindesaurus was discovered near Chinde Point in Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, by Bryan Small in 1984.
facts.quote: El espécimen holotipo de Chindesaurus, un esqueleto parcial, fue hallado cerca de Punto Chinde en el Parque nacional del Bosque Petrificado, Arizona, por Bryan Small en 1984.

facts.statement: The genus name Chindesaurus is derived from the Navajo word chindi, meaning "ghost" or "evil spirit", and the Greek word sauros, meaning "lizard".
facts.quote: El nombre del género Chindesaurus se deriva de la palabra navajo chindi que significa "fantasma" o "espíritu maligno" y la palabra griega "sauros", σαυρος, que significa "lagarto".

facts.statement: The specific name C. bryansmalli honors the discoverer, Bryan Small.
facts.quote: El nombre específico , C. bryansmalli honra al descubridor, Bryan Small.

facts.statement: Chindesaurus was described and named by R. A. Long and P. A. Murry in 1995.
facts.quote: Chindesaurus fue descrito y nombrado por R. A. Long y P. A. Murry, en 1995

facts.statement: The most complete specimen, PEFO 10395, includes a single tooth, fragmentary neck and back vertebrae, rib fragments, two complete hip vertebrae, fragmentary tail vertebrae, a chevron, fragmentary hip bones, a complete left femur, a fragmentary right femur, a fragmentary right tibia, and a right ankle bone.
facts.quote: El tipo PEFO 10395 es el más completo, que consta de un solo diente, una vértebra fragmentaria del cuello, vértebras fragmentaria del lomo, varios fragmentos de costillas, dos vértebras completas de las caderas, vértebras caudales fragmentarias, un cheurón , varios huesos de la cadera fragmentarios, un fémur izquierdo completo y un fémur derecho fragmentario, una tibia derecha fragmentaria y un hueso del tobillo derecho.

facts.statement: The type and paratype specimens were approximately 2 to 2.3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Los especímenes de tipo y paratipo tenían aproximadamente 2 a 2,3 metros de longitud.

facts.statement: Some estimates suggest that Chindesaurus weighed a maximum of 50 kilograms.
facts.quote: Algunas estimaciones sugieren que Chindesaurus pesaba 50 kilogramos como máximo.

facts.statement: The ancient floodplain environment where Chindesaurus lived also contained abundant lungfish and clams.
facts.quote: This paleoenvironment also had abundant lungfish and clams.

facts.statement: Chindesaurus is classified within the family Herrerasauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Herrerasauridae

facts.statement: The genus authority for Chindesaurus is Long & Murry, 1995.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Long & Murry, 1995

facts.statement: In a 2007 article, Nesbitt, Irmis, and Parker agreed that there were few reasons to separate Caseosaurus from Chindesaurus, as the two shared unique characteristics not found in similar species.
facts.quote: Nesbitt, Irmis y Parker estuvieron de acuerdo en un artículo de 2007 que había pocas razones para separar a Caseosaurus de Chindesaurus, y los dos incluso compartían características únicas no halladas en especies similares.

facts.statement: However, because both species are so fragmentary, researchers decided not to formally make them synonyms.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, dado que ambas especies son tan fragmentarias, ellos decidieron no hacerlos sinónimos formalmente.

facts.statement: According to Nesbitt, Irmis, and Parker, the affinities of Chindesaurus cannot be verified due to the great similarity of preserved parts with Saturnalia and the absence of much of the skeleton.
facts.quote: Según ellos actualmente, las afinidades de Chindesaurus no se pueden verificar debido a la gran semejanza de las partes preservadas con Saturnalia y la ausencia de gran parte del esqueleto.

facts.statement: A 2011 phylogenetic analysis by Sues, Nesbitt, Berman, and Henrici indicated that Chindesaurus is a herrerasaurid theropod.
facts.quote: El siguiente es un cladograma basado en el análisis filogenético de Hans-Dieter Sues, Sterling J. Nesbitt, David S Berman y Amy C. Henrici, en 2011, que indicó que Chindesaurus es un terópodo herrerasáurido.

facts.statement: The fossil record for Chindesaurus spans from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago during the Norian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Norian (227.3 to 205.7 million years ago)
